title: The Delightful History of Pubs
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the British and Irish pub, from Roman-era taverns marked by grapevines and bushes, through Anglo-Saxon ale wives and ale stakes, King Edward's regulation of drinking places and peg tankards, Irish hospitality laws and the Coroners Act, the gin craze and Hogarth's Beer Street and Gin Lane, Victorian gin palaces, pub names and pub games (darts, skittles, bat and trap), American taverns like Manuel's Tavern and Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop, and the decline of pubs through tied houses and pub companies. The episode closes with a listener mail about land acknowledgements.
topics: King Edward the Peaceful drinking laws

segments.title: Opening banter about favorite old pubs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share memories of old, characterful pubs in Manchester and Dublin and introduce the idea that pubs are essential to England and Ireland, with a Belloc quote.

segments.title: Roman taverns and Anglo-Saxon ale
segments.summary: Romans ran taverns along their roads, marked by grapevines and later bushes in Britain. The Anglo-Saxons preferred ale, which had no hops; hops came later, and ale wives brewed for travelers, marking their houses with an ale stake.

segments.title: Drinking regulation under King Edward and peg tankards
segments.summary: King Edward the Peaceful is said to have started early laws regulating drinking places, calling for at least one in every town, and limiting drinking with the peg tankard.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before moving to Ireland.

segments.title: Irish hospitality law and licensing in England
segments.summary: Irish law required hospitality to travelers, including always-ready ale and food. Between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries, ale houses, taverns and inns became licensed, and brewing passed from women to men.

segments.title: Gin craze, Hogarth prints, and Victorian gin palaces
segments.summary: Gin was vilified in the eighteenth century, and Hogarth's Beer Street and Gin Lane contrast beer and gin. Gin returned in the nineteenth century, prompting gin palaces and the addition of bars to pubs. The Coroners Act of 1846 led some Irish pubs to hold bodies, and an 1870s law's three-mile loophole let pubs open past closing.

segments.title: Pubs in America and famous old taverns
segments.summary: Irish immigrants brought pub culture to America. Hosts discuss Manuel's Tavern in Atlanta, the White Horse Tavern in Newport, Fraunces Tavern in New York, and Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop in New Orleans.

segments.title: Pub names and pub games
segments.summary: Pub names began as hanging signs for illiterate customers and often reflect local and national history. Examples include the Cat and Fiddle, Bag of Nails, Crown, Red Lion, and Royal Oak. Darts is discussed with its archery origins, plus skittles and bat and trap.

segments.title: Decline of pubs: tied houses and pub companies
segments.summary: Brewers' tied houses in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries limited pubs to one brand, and later pub companies bought up pubs as real estate. The 2007 smoking ban and the coronavirus lockdowns hurt pubs. The Campaign for Real Ale keeps a guide to traditional pubs.

segments.title: Oldest pubs in England
segments.summary: The Old Fighting Cocks, Shakespeare's Head (Shawn's Bar per transcript), and Old Ferry Boat Inn are discussed as candidates for the oldest pub in England.

segments.title: Listener mail on land acknowledgements
segments.summary: Listener Ron G suggests land acknowledgements, citing a Buddhist temple seminar in Sacramento; the hosts say they have seen them on tour in Australia and New Zealand.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts encourage support for local independent pubs and invite listener mail.
